heatflow.label: Surface heat flow (mW/m²)
heatflow.explain: Heat flowing out of the Earth's crust, in milliwatts per square metre - the most direct physical indicator of geothermal energy moving toward the surface. Continental background is ~40-65; above ~80 is notable; above ~100 marks geothermal provinces like the Great Basin and Imperial Valley.

source.name: SMU Geothermal Lab national heat-flow database (DOE Geothermal Data Repository, submission 1704), 58,117 well observations

gradient.label: Geothermal gradient (°C/km)
gradient.explain: How quickly temperature rises with depth. The continental average is ~25 °C/km; higher gradients mean useful temperatures at shallower - and much cheaper - drilling depths. Values above ~50 °C/km generally justify geothermal exploration.

source.name: SMU Geothermal Lab database (DOE GDR submission 1704), 102,751 corrected well gradients

temp3km.label: Est. temperature at 3 km (°C)
temp3km.explain: Estimated rock temperature at 3 km depth, extended linearly from measured gradients (T = 15 °C + gradient x 3 km, capped at 400 °C). 150 °C or more is the conventional threshold for flash-steam power; 90-150 °C suits binary-cycle plants and direct use. 3 km is a routinely drillable depth.

source.name: Derived by this project from the SMU gradient grid (DOE GDR submission 1704)

temp5km.label: Est. temperature at 5 km (°C)
temp5km.explain: Same derivation at 5 km - the frontier depth for enhanced geothermal systems (EGS). Where 3 km is too cool, adequate temperature at 5 km signals EGS potential with deeper drilling.

source.name: Derived by this project from the SMU gradient grid (DOE GDR submission 1704)

st_temp3km.label: Temperature at 3 km — Stanford ML model (°C)
st_temp3km.explain: Machine-learning prediction of temperature at 3 km depth from the Stanford Thermal Earth Model (Aljubran & Horne, 2024) - a modern national model trained on bottom-hole temperatures plus geophysical and geological features (~4 km native resolution). More reliable than linear gradient extrapolation, especially in hydrothermal areas.

source.name: Stanford Thermal Earth Model (DOE GDR submission 1592), 534,942 model points

st_temp5km.label: Temperature at 5 km — Stanford ML model (°C)
st_temp5km.explain: Stanford Thermal Earth Model prediction at 5 km - the EGS frontier depth. Where 3 km is too cool, adequate temperature at 5 km signals EGS potential with deeper drilling.

source.name: Stanford Thermal Earth Model (DOE GDR submission 1592)

gb_p50.label: Hydrothermal favorability (Great Basin percentile)
gb_p50.explain: USGS machine-learning prediction (2025, INGENIOUS project) of how favorable conditions are for undiscovered conventional hydrothermal systems, combining heat, active faulting, seismicity and groundwater signals. Shown as a percentile within the Great Basin: 90 means more favorable than 90% of the region. Covers the Great Basin only (NV + margins).

source.name: USGS Great Basin geothermal favorability (P50 estimate), DOI 10.5066/P14EET2C

heatflow.note: IDW (k=12, power=2.0) of SMU/GDR-1704 well observations onto a 0.05 deg grid; cells farther than 120.0 km from any well are masked.

gradient.note: Same IDW parameters; corrected interval gradients preferred.

temp3km.note: DERIVED: T(z) = 15.0 C + gradient x depth, capped at 400 C. A linear extrapolation of shallow gradients - unreliable in convection-dominated hydrothermal fields, effective resolution tens of km; ranks areas, does not derisk parcels.

st_temp3km.label: Temperature at 3 km — Stanford ML model (°C)
st_temp3km.explain: Machine-learning prediction of temperature at 3 km depth from the Stanford Thermal Earth Model (Aljubran & Horne, 2024) - a modern national model trained on bottom-hole temperatures plus geophysical and geological features (~4 km native resolution). More reliable than linear gradient extrapolation, especially in hydrothermal areas.

source.name: Stanford Thermal Earth Model (DOE GDR submission 1592), 534,942 model points

st_temp5km.label: Temperature at 5 km — Stanford ML model (°C)
st_temp5km.explain: Stanford Thermal Earth Model prediction at 5 km - the EGS frontier depth. Where 3 km is too cool, adequate temperature at 5 km signals EGS potential with deeper drilling.

source.name: Stanford Thermal Earth Model (DOE GDR submission 1592)

gb_p50.note: USGS ML hydrothermal favorability P50 (250 m native), area-averaged to the working grid and expressed as a percentile of the Great Basin distribution. Null outside the Great Basin study area.
